verdict.tagline: Brutal dungeon crawling wrapped in stunning gothic atmosphere and unrelenting chance.
for_you_if: you enjoy punishing tactical challenges and dark fantasy
you appreciate deep party stress and resource management
you welcome community mods to expand your experience
not_for_you_if: you cannot stand losing characters to random chance
you get frustrated by steep learning curves
you are looking for a forgiving dungeon crawler

Honestly I love it!! I really enjoy how newbies (like myself) are introduced to the game and its mechanics!! It gives you tips when something new starts to happen!! I also love that each hero has different personalities and quirks, both negative and positive!! I don't love my character dying (haven't died yet, fingers crossed) but I do think it adds to the stakes of the game!! I absolutely LOVE the art style and found out about this game through a professor of mine! I will say that each short mission is about 30-40 minutes so it definitely takes a bit but I think its nice because you can come back to it whenever you want, do a quest and take a break :)) I think everything makes you root for the characters in your party, even with the little dialogue they say on their own!! Genuinely had me stressing when a character was panicking about dying and expressed it in the chat bubbles and actions and I really feel like that was a really neat touch!!

Only negative thing I'd say is that it can be a veryyyy stressful game since the mechanic of "stress" and "light" correspond with each other from what I've seen so far. If you don't bring enough food or torches, or bandages then your party genuinely might get wiped </3 With the stress getting too high, the characters die forever and thats it. I do like that you are able to get more characters but I do think this is definitely something I play a little bit at a time because of that. However, you are able to cure your characters from their ailments and stresses during your down time outside of the dungeons and quests!! 

I'd definitely rate this game a 7.5/10!! I'm not super used to turn based combat games as an MMORPG player but I really feel like this is a fun refreshing game beyond that one negative I mentioned :)
Stress Simulator. Lovely art direction, lovely AND IINFURIATING gameplay. And an absolutely pristine narration. Rest in Peace, Wayne June, you will be sorely missed.
Lots of darkness and samey atmosphere. Difficult, stressful, a bit boring.
What the hell is with the difficulty? I don't know if I'm just very unfortunate or what but I lost all my money and every new recruit sucks and I cant get past the second mission.

The artstyle, the mechanics (I haven't completed the *entire* tutorial so take that with a spoon of salt), the LORE (I bought the game because of the lore)... I can't play this game because I don't have the mental for it. Every pawn I recruit, every thing I get, I get attached to them. So when they die, it's a personal insult, attack and a slap in the face.

Again, the game is good but prepare to lose people, equipment, expeditions and even campaigns. Otherwise you wouldn't be able to enjoy it to the fullest.

Definitely an interesting and fun idea but I can't stand what this game does to me.
I started a new game, finished the tutorial without incident and completed my first mission doing very well. At the Hamlet I recruited two more heroes and departed once more. On my second mission in the first combat encounter, my Vestal missed every attack and my team got critted twice in 4 rounds. Heavy damage but I could still recover from it. Second encounter I got the surprise on the enemy but it didn't matter because half my team missed and the enemy crit me again on the first round. By round 4 I had barely won but the expedition was doomed due to the enemies criting another four times in that duration. I pressed on and predictably wiped. With only two heroes left my first campaign was basically over after two deployments.
Similarly unlucky events occurred in the two campaigns that followed. They also ended still in the metaphorical womb.
This game has no concept of balance. Even with the prior knowledge of watching dozens of videos on it, following guides, and paying attention to stats and chances of success it didn't help me enough. And what can when the lowest level enemies in the game have such a high potential for game ending damage? I enjoy a good dice roll occasionally but as someone who usually has supernaturally bad luck this game does not let you cope around it. There is no reloading, no quick-saving or do-overs; why? For the sake of permadeath mattering.
It doesn't help that there seems to be an amount of elitism surrounding this game with many just saying "you get used to it" or "It gets better when you know what to do.". And what, pray tell, is the secret knowledge that prevents a 15% chance to die on quest two?
I've always hated gambling and chance games because house always wins, especially in my case it seems. If this game let me choose when it saved perhaps I'd be more merciful in my review but it showed me none so what reason should I?

claims.claim: Reviewers note that character management and progression involve handling stress levels and afflictions where heroes can gain debuffs or mental conditions when reaching maximum stress.

citations.review_text:
This game will break your mind, but you'll keep coming back for more.
Forget RPGs that handhold you Darkest Dungeon 1 is a masterclass in tactical depth. If you want punishing mechanics where every decision actually matters, this is it.
Why the mechanics and gameplay are brilliant:
1. Stress & Affliction System : HP isn't your only resource. At 100 Stress, heroes break—gaining game-ruining debuffs (Paranoid, Abusive) or clutch buffs (Virtue). Managing mental health adds a whole new tactical layer.
2. Strict Positioning : Formations (Ranks 1–4) determine which skills you can use and target. Enemy shuffles force you to build flexible comps and adapt on the fly when your plan collapses.
3. Deep Synergies : Comp building is insanely rewarding, whether you stack DoTs (Bleed/Blight), run Mark burst squads, or abuse Stun mechanics to control enemy turn economy.
4. Risk Mitigation over Luck : RNG exists, but the skill lies in minimizing risk. You constantly weigh torchlight levels (safe light vs. high-risk/high-reward darkness) and build squads to survive worst-case scenarios.
5. Cold Estate Management :  Heroes are disposable tools. Upgrading the Hamlet gives permanent progression even when a squad wipes, forcing tough macro-decisions on who to cure and who to replace.
Darkest Dungeon 1 rewards strategy and adaptability. Victories are never handed to you they feel earned.

I can't really recommend this game, if you don't like to be punished all the time during the game, then just buy the DD2 instead.

A tough one to review. Once I started playing it I saw what the fuss is all about and I think there is plenty that's very interesting in the game. The atmosphere, art and audio are top notch, collectively evoking that Lovecraftian sense very effectively.

I didnt click with the game in a mechanical sense, the gameplay loop of slowly upgrading shops and managing your roster should be up my street but it fell flat. I think it mostly falls down to the battles which I found uninteresting, whether the positioning of your party or the various skills that you can choose to equip, it wasnt there.

Despite my comments I think this is a good game. I have always wanted to experience what it was about and glad I did, it is however not a game I'm ready to sink the time in to completion. I give it a 6.5/10,

I originally played Darkest Dungeon on PS5. I put around 200 hours into it, and its one of the best turn based games I've ever played. The gameplay, the immersive environments, the beautifully unique art style, deep mechanics that can turn any run you do on its head in just a few turns, it all blends together to create a brutally challenging and extremely rewarding experience that I would recommend to anyone, even those who don't normally play the genre. It also has a very fun party and town management system, with rewarding progression that's easy to understand. They're usually very simple mechanics, but they still feel great to upgrade and engage with. On top of that, loads of DLC the change the game entirely, like new dungeons, heroes, stories, and way more. Darkest Dungeon is easily worth your time and money.

pain and suffering never feel this good, the art style is amazing, the RNG might be stupid some time, but the gameplay is really addicting, overall this might not for every one, but to me this game is a masterpiece

I play difficult games for a living, not really but pretend I do. This game, out of all the ones I've played, is the most sphere twisting game I've played. Normal makes me cry (metaphorically, I'm a real man). VERY repetitive game loop, but very diverse in characters, items, skills, camp skills, and probably more stuff. So, the variety more so comes from how you do stuff rather than what stuff you do. claims.claim: Reviewers describe the gameplay loop as involving town management and persistence alongside dungeon exploration.

citations.review_text: Everyone and their dog has played this, so you most likely have played this to. In the event you haven't, it's great. I played about an hour of it a long time ago and couldn't get past the fact that everyone will most likely die. I know that's part of the game, but I just couldn't warm up to it. I came back to it and now love it. Remember you are leveling up your Hamlet (town) and that's where the persistence factors in. Remember, even if your best character died, you still have the Hamlet which is advancing.

One of the truly masterful entries in the genre, I think this is one of the best games for illustrating how far style & flavour goes in design. The narrators epic, booming voice and verbose narration makes any moment (no matter how frustrating or annoying) feel exciting. The design of all the horrible, eldritch & terrifying creatures throughout engages you, even when your Barbarian refuses to actually pull-off the clutch save you're needing. Finding torches, food and bandages in those clutch moments that allow you to make it to the final boss, only to get skewered because your healers kept getting shuffled into the wrong place. Every little moment of this game is drenched in style, dripping with world-building flavour, and makes those exciting moments feel epic, and those damned moments feel thriling enough to go again.

I think the loop itself is very simple. Town, stock up, recover the sanity of your team, go out and try maintain a careful balance of sanity, resources & wealth. Kill some freaky dudes, come across horrible abominations roaming the halls, make sacrifices and experience heroic moments or your own team daming you to Hell, and then kill the most disgusting beast you've ever seen. Back to town and do it all again! The two main DLCs (Court & Colour) add just enough to create strange variety while still keeping this core loop in tact. 

Red Hook really made something special here, and I will forever love it.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that character progression persists through the upgrading of the town or hamlet rather than individual hero levels.

citations.review_text: Everyone and their dog has played this, so you most likely have played this to. In the event you haven't, it's great. I played about an hour of it a long time ago and couldn't get past the fact that everyone will most likely die. I know that's part of the game, but I just couldn't warm up to it. A lot of people believe this game to be impossible to complete. Indeed there is only a less than 5% completion rate if the global achievements screen is to be believed. I was one of those people until I watched a few videos that changed my perspective. These videos were not tutorials but rather an exploration of the theme and how the game changes you as the player the longer you play it.

The winning attitude for this title is that your heroes are a means to an end. They are only as valuable as the money and trinkets you have invested in them. They are meant to be expended in order to further the game. This doesn't mean to waste them, but rather to understand when they die and a party gets wiped, that isn't the end to the run. The real run progression lies elsewhere.

This game changes you as someone who values human life, even that of the npcs, to a manager of a dangerous venture. Everything and everyone slowly becomes a name or a number. The game molds you into the likeness of the estates original proprietor, your ancestor. Someone who would pay humans to break themselves whether willing or unwilling so that you can further your own goals. The true progression in this game is the collection of money, trinkets, and upgrades. The buildings you build in the hamlet are the proof of your advancement, not necessarily the levels on the heroes. 

The bottom-line is you concern, is it possible to complete the run so that you get return on investment? Or do you have to cut your losses? Not to only preserve the lives of your party but more importantly the money you put into their skills in equipment. Losses can be absorbed, money recovered, and the heroes never stop showing up. Progress is backtracked only in the loss of money and having to fill a hero slot with some fresh face unaccustomed to the bleak and hopeless trek this whole ordeal is. 

Prose aside, this game is a lot of fun and it is stressful. But you don't have to worry about losing the game if your party gets wip…

Ultimately you end up just totally disconnecting from the characters and they all just become meat thrown into a grinder, throwing them in without supplies or anything and once they are max stress and have 500 negative quirks and diseases you throw them out, if they don't die before that, and just recruit a new one to throw to their death for free. After all fixing characters of their stress and quirks is a long and tedius and ultimately too expensive process.
In other hard games it can be easy to become attached to a character and its class but with how easily and quickly these ones become rotten with quirks or die to a random encounter that had no forewarning its just not worth it, just send them in to get 1 heirloom or 100 gold then throw them in a bin.

I expected a lovecraftian esque gothic horror with some people dying, I didn't expect to be playing Gothic Soviet Simulator wave assaulting eldritch horrors.

A lot of people believe this game to be impossible to complete. Indeed there is only a less than 5% completion rate if the global achievements screen is to be believed. I was one of those people until I watched a few videos that changed my perspective. These videos were not tutorials but rather an exploration of the theme and how the game changes you as the player the longer you play it.

The winning attitude for this title is that your heroes are a means to an end. They are only as valuable as the money and trinkets you have invested in them. They are meant to be expended in order to further the game. This doesn't mean to waste them, but rather to understand when they die and a party gets wiped, that isn't the end to the run. The real run progression lies elsewhere.

This game changes you as someone who values human life, even that of the npcs, to a manager of a dangerous venture. Everything and everyone slowly becomes a name or a number. The game molds you into the likeness of the estates original proprietor, your ancestor. Someone who would pay humans to break themselves whether willing or unwilling so that you can further your own goals. The true progression in this game is the collection of money, trinkets, and upgrades. The buildings you build in the hamlet are the proof of your advancement, not necessarily the levels on the heroes. 

The bottom-line is you concern, is it possible to complete the run so that you get return on investment? Or do you have to cut your losses? Not to only preserve the lives of your party but more importantly the money you put into their skills in equipment. Losses can be absorbed, money recovered, and the heroes never stop showing up. Progress is backtracked only in the loss of money and having to fill a hero slot with some fresh face unaccustomed to the bleak and hopeless trek this whole ordeal is. 

Prose aside, this game is a lot of fun and it is stressful. But you don't have to worry about losing the game if your party gets wip…

One of the truly masterful entries in the genre, I think this is one of the best games for illustrating how far style & flavour goes in design. The narrators epic, booming voice and verbose narration makes any moment (no matter how frustrating or annoying) feel exciting. The design of all the horrible, eldritch & terrifying creatures throughout engages you, even when your Barbarian refuses to actually pull-off the clutch save you're needing. Finding torches, food and bandages in those clutch moments that allow you to make it to the final boss, only to get skewered because your healers kept getting shuffled into the wrong place. Every little moment of this game is drenched in style, dripping with world-building flavour, and makes those exciting moments feel epic, and those damned moments feel thriling enough to go again.

I think the loop itself is very simple. Town, stock up, recover the sanity of your team, go out and try maintain a careful balance of sanity, resources & wealth. Kill some freaky dudes, come across horrible abominations roaming the halls, make sacrifices and experience heroic moments or your own team daming you to Hell, and then kill the most disgusting beast you've ever seen. Back to town and do it all again! The two main DLCs (Court & Colour) add just enough to create strange variety while still keeping this core loop in tact. 

Red Hook really made something special here, and I will forever love it.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that dungeon runs and combat can feel slow, repetitive, or bogged down by specific mechanics like shuffling and traps.

citations.review_text:
The game is not good, like at all: 4/10

TL;DR: Dont waste your time, play something better.

Reddit touted how amazing it is, and it looked quite interesting visually and from the descriptions so i tried it... a lot...

Its just not a good game.

There are way too many character values that dont respond or work like they seem and there is no explanation how they actually work, even searching online brings you nowhere, because the functionality of most stats changed vastly over the years and patches.

Characters die constantly, which feels awful, because death being a threat is one thing, but you can literally die in a single enemy turn with no way to prepare, load or escape.

Most of the story is just repeating miscellaneous quests with no interesting writing or anything.

The combat itself is convoluted and complex for the sake of complexity with no sense, there would be so many ways to streamline the stats and functionality to make it make more sense and just be better, but they chose not to.

The actual dungeon runs are slow, with most "encounters" i.e. objects you find not doing anything but being traps in disguise, so just ignore them.

Traps are also often unavoidable even if detected and prepared for.

The random dungeon map sounds fun at first, but once you see that you can run into a deadend and then slowly with a lot of loading screens have to go back THROUGH ALL ROOMS AND WALKWAYS YOU ALREADY WENT THROUGH WITH NOTHING NEW HAPPENING you see how much time is wasted literally doing nothing but walking.

Seriously, the game is a severe disappointment and utter waste of time.

I 100% the game because i wanted to give it a fair chance, but even with various mods and following dedicated builds to reduce strain it still took me way too long to get through this slog of a game...

The battle is sooooo slow. And the stress mechanic is ridiculous. I get that it's supposed to be hard, but it's unreasonably hard. I get that positioning is a key tactic point, but why does moving takes up a whole turn, just for every boss to shuffle it again next turn. It's more frustrating to play and to bare than enjoying

I didn't like it, but it's a good game.

I'm giving Darkest Dungeon a positive review because even though I had a miserable time, I don't think the game was bad. DD is very good at what it's supposed to be, but it wasn't for me. There was too much micromanagement, and repetitiveness. I just found myself annoyed most of the time instead enjoying myself.

I was going to write a long review but I decided it wasn't worth the effort. If you want a challenging game that has a lot of different characters, items, quirks, and skills to choose from where the odds are stacked against you - and you have to struggle through every dungeon, then it's a good game.

If you want a turn based game where you get stronger and better and eventually feel like you can take on the world, this isn't it. Almost every fight was hard, or frustrating, or unfair. Most of the enemies are designed to make your time as miserable as possible, and to the game's credit, that fits perfectly, but it was just frustrating to me.

I didn't look up any strategy guides, I went in blind. I enjoyed the first 15 or 20 hours, but there came a point where I was just brute forcing my way through because I got bored of fighting the exact same fights and dealing with the inventory and stress mechanics.

My town was almost fully upgraded and I had a bunch of level 5 characters and a few level 6. I just got past my first year and decided to give up because I just felt like I wasn't any stronger or better than when I first started. Every dungeon was stressful and it always felt like I was going to lose, but usually I would pull through... but sitting there, trying to play a game for hours at a time just to feel like you barely made it, struggling and suffering and losing just to win at the very end never really felt satisfying or cathartic, I just felt like I was always doing something wrong the whole time.

Sometimes it's okay to give up, not all games are made for everybody, and this one is certainly not made for me.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game heavily relies on random chance and dice rolls, which can ruin a well-prepared run.

citations.review_text:
I tried my hardest to enjoy it. However, the game made it impossible. 

Wheras the gameplay loop is very enjoyable, and on the surface this type of game should be right up my alley, the RNG elements just take all the fun out of the experience. 
Maybe I'm just a particularily unlucky, but in my experience the game the game simply renders your preparations meaningless. 
There never comes a point where your hard work pays off. 
No matter how well prepared you are, no matter what you do, no matter what strategy you take, the roll of a dice holds absolute power over the results. 

You can level up all your heroes, give them the best gear, the best abilities, remove all their negative quirks, make them almost overqualified for the mission, and prepare more supplies than are needed. 
All of that, and you may still watch them all perish, because you were unlucky. 

This has been a huge waste of time.

After 30 hours, I'm still having a miserable time. It's fun.

Jokes aside, the game has a steep learning curve. But once you start getting a grasp of the game's mechanics, get over getting some of your heroes killed and learn when to abandon a quest, the game becomes a lot more manageable.

One major turn off for me is how much of a dice roll everything is. You can enter a quest well prepared and knowledgeable, but your run can be ruined by plain bad RNG. But the game rewards tenacity and learning. Even devastating setbacks can be overcome.

It is a fun and engaging game. And I recommend anyone who likes to challenge themselves and overcome adversity to play the game.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as heavily reliant on RNG and random number generation, which can cause expeditions or characters to fail regardless of player preparation.

citations.review_text:
My experience with the Darkest Dungeon can be likened to a really dizzying rollercoaster ride. I received the game from a great friend of mine and decided to go in completely blind to the experience. On my initial playthrough I quickly fell in love with the amazing hand-drawn artstyle, the superb Lovecraftian inspired creature and environmental design, the soundtrack and the marvelous voice acting of the Ancestor (RIP Wayne June) however, the gameplay to me was extremely decisive.

The combat looks pretty great despite the limitations of hand-drawn sprites and has a large amount of complexitiy to it. It's got all of your basic turn-based RPG elements such as stuns, debuffs, dodging, DOTs and the like. This is fine as I have played a fair amount of similar games but what Darkest Dungeon does to separate itself is taking the RNG to its true maximum. It's all about percentages. Percentage to hit, to miss, to crit, to apply DOT, to apply debuffs, to dodge and to resist an attack that would put your hero in the grave. This results in the most randomized gameplay that you could think of. Sometimes you'll crit the boss to oblivion before they even do anything special and at other times, your backliner is pulled in front and critted four times in the first fight of the dungeon. It can feel brutally unfair.

The worst thing is that progress is permanent. Your heroes level up over time, but when they die they stay dead and all of their equipment, levels, quirks, trinkets and skills are gone with them. It can be incredibly frustrating to spend multiple real life hours to painstakingly level-up a team of four heroes, only for the dice to roll against you and have your entire team die, pretty much making you lose, possibly, an entire days progress. The game will absolutely curbstomp the ♥♥♥♥ out of you if it feels like it. This is what initially made me quit the game for pretty more than half of a year.

But just like the Ancestor, there was an insistent gnawing in the back of m…

Darkest Dungeon is a fantastic game with an incredible cosmic-horror atmosphere and a richly detailed gothic, medieval aesthetic. The music, environments, enemy designs, and stress system all work together beautifully. Visually, the game feels hand-painted and made with genuine care and passion.

That said, Darkest Dungeon can also be brutally unforgiving. Sometimes it feels like an entire expedition can fall apart simply because a few things didn’t go your way. Its randomness creates a serious challenge, but it can also make the game feel unfair and frustrating. Instead of keeping you in a satisfying flow, it occasionally feels like the game is punishing you for circumstances outside your control.

Pros

- Excellent cosmic-horror atmosphere
- Beautiful hand-drawn art style
- Memorable music and sound design
- Creative and meaningful stress system
- Great enemy and environment designs
- Challenging combat that rewards careful preparation

Cons

- Heavy reliance on randomness
- A few unlucky moments can ruin an entire expedition
- Can feel unfair even when you planned carefully
- The difficulty sometimes becomes frustrating instead of satisfying
- It can be hard to settle into a consistent flow

Verdict: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆

Darkest Dungeon is a beautiful, atmospheric, and deeply memorable game. Its randomness can occasionally make the experience more frustrating than fun, but its distinctive art, brilliant atmosphere, and creative mechanics still make it absolutely worth playing.

claims.claim: Reviewers highlight the stress mechanic as a core system that requires careful management to prevent party members from suffering mental breakdowns.

citations.review_text: Though I've never beaten this game or made it through a single level of the titular darkest dungeon, I find myself coming back to this one. The characters, art, gameplay, and narration by the late and great Wayne June make it something very special. It's even still getting DLC years later, that should tell you something about how well this game has aged. Basically, you are an heir who is having to clean up the mess of your ancestor, who did a lot of crazy eldritch stuff among other things. How do you do this? By hiring a bunch of people to go out on adventures for you so you don't have to get your hands too dirty, of course! Managing the stress and health of your party members is very important; there's all kinds of nightmarish things they can encounter, like mushroom people, pig hybrids, and trapped treasure chests! There are a lot of different character classes, and each one has different pros and cons, backstories, even varying dialogue. If you're into dungeon crawlers and eldritch horror and don't mind a challenge, this is the game for you. Just don't get too attached to your party members... there are a lot of ways they can die.

play this game if you want to suffer.
the art style is amazing.
the system is unforgiving. it rules.

this game realistically depicts what happens when a group of people tilt queue on a ranked game; they stress, they start rage baiting, call names or start zoning out and become unresponsive.

but sometimes they lock in and the team comp becomes a well-oiled machine and deal with the horrors efficiently. ever had that match in an online FPS game where everything goes well and you top frag? unmatchable feeling. this game is awesome with that. there's also the other side of the coin that i mentioned beforehand; if you don't take care of your adventurers' stress, everything will go to ♥♥♥♥. a single person having their mental broken can affect the entire party. i mean, who the hell wants to queue with someone who's tilted?

seeing these characters react to the world and react accordingly is so cool.
game is enhanced with mods!!!
game is hard.
don't rage quit, you got this!!!

But just like the Ancestor, there was an insistent gnawing in the back of m…

[h1][b]Recommended[/b][/h1]

Darkest Dungeon is still one of my favourite roguelike dungeon crawlers ever made, and years later I still haven't found another game that does everything quite as well.

At first glance it looks like a simple turn-based RPG, but it quickly becomes much more than that. Every expedition feels like a gamble. You're constantly balancing resources, stress, injuries, diseases, and the growing possibility that one bad decision could cost you a character you've spent hours building.

[b]Atmosphere[/b]

The atmosphere is easily one of the game's strongest features. The art style is fantastic, the soundtrack is memorable, and the narration from the Ancestor has become iconic for a reason. Every dungeon feels oppressive, and the game constantly reminds you that survival is never guaranteed.

Few games have managed to make me feel genuine dread from opening a door or investigating a seemingly harmless object.

[b]Gameplay[/b]

The combat is simple to learn but has an incredible amount of depth. Team composition matters, positioning matters, and understanding how different classes work together can mean the difference between success and disaster.

What I love most is that failure is part of the experience. Heroes die. Plans fall apart. Entire expeditions can collapse because of a single mistake or a streak of terrible luck. Instead of feeling unfair, it usually makes victory feel even more rewarding.

[b]"Be wary, overconfidence is a slow, and insidious killer"[/b]

Darkest Dungeon is brutal, stressful, and occasionally cruel.

It's also one of the best dungeon crawlers ever made.

If you enjoy challenging turn-based combat, incredible atmosphere, and games that create memorable stories through both success and failure, I highly recommend it.
